title.en: Cheops the Tyrant: Ten Years on the Causeway

region.en: Giza, Egypt (the great pyramid and its causeway)
region.zh: 埃及吉薩（大金字塔與其石道）

texts.period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.124-125 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 124-125

summary.en: The priests' curse-memory of the pyramid age: Cheops shut the temples, stopped the sacrifices, and drove every Egyptian to labour for him — a hundred thousand men at a time, three months each, ten years for the causeway alone and twenty for the pyramid — and the Egyptians, hating him, refuse even to name the kings, calling the pyramids after the shepherd Philitis.
summary.zh: 祭司所詛之金字塔時代：胡夫閉神廟、禁祭品、驅全民為其勞作——每批十萬人，三月一換，僅石道即築十年，塔又二十年——埃及人恨之入骨，拒呼王名，而以牧人菲利提斯之名稱金字塔。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Herodotus' hostile account is a literary tradition, not an archaeological record.

passages.text: Down to the time when Rhampsinitos was king, they told me there was in Egypt nothing but orderly rule, and Egypt prospered greatly; but after him Cheops became king over them and brought them to every kind of evil: for he shut up all the temples, and having first kept them from sacrificing there, he then bade all the Egyptians work for him. So some were appointed to draw stones from the stone-quarries in the Arabian mountains to the Nile, and others he ordered to receive the stones after they had been carried over the river in boats, and to draw them to those which are called the Libyan mountains; and they worked by a hundred thousand men at a time, for each three months continually.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.124.

passages.text: Of this oppression there passed ten years while the causeway was made by which they drew the stones, which causeway they built, and it is a work not much less, as it appears to me, than the pyramid; for the length of it is five furlongs and the breadth ten fathoms and the height, where it is highest, eight fathoms, and it is made of stone smoothed and with figures carved upon it. For the making of the pyramid itself there passed a period of twenty years; and the pyramid is square, each side measuring eight hundred feet, and the height of it is the same.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.124.

passages.text: Here then they reckon one hundred and six years, during which they say that there was nothing but evil for the Egyptians, and the temples were kept closed and not opened during all that time. These kings the Egyptians by reason of their hatred of them are not very willing to name; nay, they even call the pyramids after the name of Philitis the shepherd, who at that time pastured flocks in those regions.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.128.

title.en: The King's Daughter and Her Pyramid of Stones

region.en: Giza, Egypt (the middle of the three queens' pyramids, one side 150 feet)
region.zh: 埃及吉薩（三后金字塔之中者，每邊一百五十英尺）

texts.period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.126 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 126

summary.en: Driven to want of money, Cheops sent his own daughter to the stews; she not only raised the appointed sum but asked each visitor for one stone toward her building — and of these stones, the Egyptians told Herodotus, the middle of the three small pyramids was built, one hundred and fifty feet on every side.
summary.zh: 胡夫財匱，遣親女入妓院斂金；女不但足額，更向每位客人索一石以備營造——埃及人告希羅多德：此三小金字塔中間之一，即以此諸石砌成，每邊一百五十英尺。

sensitivity.note: Ancient folk aition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Cheops moreover came, they said, to such a pitch of wickedness, that being in want of money he caused his own daughter to sit in the stews, and ordered her to obtain from those who came a certain amount of money (how much it was they did not tell me); but she not only obtained the sum appointed by her father, but also she formed a design for herself privately to leave behind her a memorial, and she requested each man who came in to her to give her one stone upon her building: and of these stones, they told me, the pyramid was built which stands in front of the great pyramid in the middle of the three, each side being one hundred and fifty feet in length.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.126.

title.en: Mycerinus and the Golden Cow: The Sun Once a Year
title.zh: 門卡烏拉與金牛：歲見日光一次

region.en: Sais, Western Delta, Egypt (the royal palace chamber of the gilded cow)
region.zh: 埃及西三角洲薩伊斯（王宮鍍金牛之室）

texts.period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.129-132 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 129-132

summary.en: The just king Mycerinus loses his only daughter and buries her in a hollow cow of wood covered with gold; the rival tale makes him her lover and the girl strangled herself — her mother cutting off the hands of the maids who betrayed her, hence the handless colossi; the cow still stood at Sais in Herodotus' day, carried into the sunlight once a year, for the daughter dying asked to see the sun once in the year.
summary.zh: 賢王門卡烏拉喪獨女，製中空鍍金牛以葬之；異聞謂王亂其女，女自縊，母斷洩密侍女之手——故其裸體巨像皆無手。此牛至希羅多德時仍陳於薩伊斯，歲一出室見日一次——蓋女臨終求其父：歲見日光一次。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: But while Mykerinos was acting mercifully to his subjects and practising this conduct which has been said, calamities befell him, of which the first was this, namely that his daughter died, the only child whom he had in his house: and being above measure grieved by that which had befallen him, and desiring to bury his daughter in a manner more remarkable than others, he made a cow of wood, which he covered over with gold, and then within it he buried this daughter who, as I said, had died.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.129.

passages.text: Some however tell about this cow and the colossal statues the following tale, namely that Mykerinos was enamoured of his own daughter and afterwards ravished her; and upon this they say that the girl strangled herself for grief, and he buried her in this cow; and her mother cut off the hands of the maids who had betrayed the daughter to her father; wherefore now the images of them have suffered that which the maids suffered in their life. In thus saying they speak idly, as it seems to me, especially in what they say about the hands of the statues; for as to this, even we ourselves saw that their hands had dropped off from lapse of time.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.131.

passages.text: The cow is covered up with a crimson robe, except only the head and the neck, which are seen, overlaid with gold very thickly; and between the horns there is the disc of the sun figured in gold. The cow is not standing up but kneeling, and in size it is equal to a large living cow. Every year it is carried forth from the chamber... for they say that she asked of her father Mykerinos, when she was dying, that she might look upon the sun once in the year.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.132.

title.en: Mycerinus Defies the Oracle: Nights Made into Days
title.zh: 門卡烏拉抗神諭：以夜為晝

region.en: Buto, Nile Delta, Egypt (the oracle that doomed a just king)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布托（判賢王短命之神諭）

texts.period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.133 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 133

summary.en: An oracle from Buto gives the pious Mycerinus six years only — while his impious father and uncle had reigned long; he sends a reproach to the god and receives back the terrible answer: it is precisely his justice that hastens the end, for Egypt is doomed to suffer one hundred and fifty years. So the king lights lamps every night and lives a life of pleasure night and day, turning night into day to prove the oracle false.
summary.zh: 布托神諭判虔敬之王門卡烏拉僅餘六年——而其不敬之父叔皆長壽；王遣使責神，復得駭人回語：正因爾之公義，故速爾之終——埃及當受一百五十年之災。王遂夜夜燃燈，晝夜行樂，以夜作晝，欲證神諭之妄。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: An oracle came to him from the city of Buto, saying that he was destined to live but six years more, in the seventh year to end his life: and he being indignant at it sent to the Oracle a reproach against the god, making complaint in reply that whereas his father and uncle, who had shut up the temples and had not only not remembered the gods, but also had been destroyers of men, had lived for a long time, he himself, who practised piety, was destined to end his life so soon: and from the Oracle there came a second message, which said that it was for this very cause that he was bringing his life to a swift close; for he had not done that which it was appointed for him to do, since it was destined that Egypt should suffer evils for a hundred and fifty years, and the two kings who had risen before him had perceived this, but he had not.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.133.

passages.text: Mykerinos having heard this, and considering that this sentence had been passed upon him beyond recall, procured many lamps, and whenever night came on he lighted these and began to drink and take his pleasure, ceasing neither by day nor by night; and he went about to the fen-country and to the woods and wherever he heard there were the most suitable places for enjoyment. This he devised (having a mind to prove that the Oracle spoke falsely) in order that he might have twelve years of life instead of six, the nights being turned into days.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.133.

title.en: Sabacos' Dream: The Ethiopian Who Refused to Cut the Priests
title.zh: 薩巴科斯之夢：不肯割裂祭司的埃塞俄比亞王

region.en: Egypt under Ethiopian rule, capital at Memphis (Sabacos' fifty years)
region.zh: 埃塞俄比亞統治下的埃及（薩巴科斯五十年）

texts.period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.137-140 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 137-140

summary.en: Sabacos the Ethiopian rules Egypt for fifty years, never putting a wrongdoer to death but setting each to raise an embankment around his own city; then a dream stands by him counselling the impious deed of cutting all Egypt's priests in two, and he reads it as the gods' snare: his prophesied fifty years are expired — he departs of his own free will.
summary.zh: 埃塞俄比亞王薩巴科斯治埃及五十年，從不誅犯者，而令各就其城築堤贖罪；後夢中一人立於身側，勸其割裂全埃及之祭司——王悟為神之誘餌，且其神諭之五十年已滿，遂自願離國而去。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In his reign the Ethiopians and Sabacos the king of the Ethiopians marched upon Egypt with a great host of men; so this blind man departed, flying to the fen-country, and the Ethiopian was king over Egypt for fifty years, during which he performed deeds as follows: — whenever any man of the Egyptians committed any transgression, he would never put him to death, but he gave sentence upon each man according to the greatness of the wrong-doing, appointing them work at throwing up an embankment before that city from whence each man came of those who committed wrong. Thus the cities were made higher still than before.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.137.

passages.text: The final deliverance from the Ethiopian came about (they said) as follows: — he fled away because he had seen in his sleep a vision, in which it seemed to him that a man came and stood by him and counselled him to gather together all the priests of Egypt and cut them asunder in the midst. Having seen this dream, he said that it seemed to him that the gods were foreshowing him this to furnish an occasion against him, in order that he might do an impious deed with respect to religion, and so receive some evil either from the gods or from men: he would not however do so, but in truth (he said) the time had expired, during which it had been prophesied to him that he should rule Egypt before he departed thence. For when he was in Ethiopia the Oracles which the Ethiopians consult had told him that it was fated for him to rule Egypt fifty years: since then this time was now expiring, and the vision of the dream also disturbed him, Sabacos departed out of Egypt of his own free will.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.139.

title.en: Sethos and the Field-Mice: The Night Egypt's Enemies Were Disarmed
title.zh: 塞托斯與田鼠：一夜之間敵軍盡失其器

region.en: Pelusium, Egypt (Sennacherib's invasion; the temple of Hephaistos/Ptah)
region.zh: 埃及佩魯西翁（辛那赫里布之侵；赫菲斯托斯/卜塔神廟）

texts.period: Priests' account of Sennacherib's campaign (c. 701 BCE), recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.141 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 141

summary.en: When Sennacherib marched on Egypt the warrior caste refused to serve the priest-king Sethos, who had stripped them of their twelve yokes of land; the king wept in the sanctuary until the god stood by him in a dream and promised helpers — and by night field-mice swarmed the Assyrian camp, eating quivers, bows and shield-handles; his statue in the temple holds a mouse: 'Let him who looks upon me learn to fear the gods.'
summary.zh: 辛那赫里布侵埃之際，被奪十二份田之戰士階層拒為祭司王塞托斯出戰；王泣於神廟聖所，夢中神立其旁許以援手——夜間田鼠蜂擁亞述營中，齧毀箭囊、弓與盾柄，敵軍赤手而潰。廟中其像手托一鼠，銘曰：『見我者當敬畏諸神。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient miracle tradition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. A cousin of the Assyrian plague-of-the-camp tradition (Herodotus here transposes 2 Kings 19).

passages.text: After this, Sanacharib king of the Arabians and of the Assyrians marched a great host against Egypt. Then the warriors of the Egyptians refused to come to the rescue, and the priest, being driven into a strait, entered into the sanctuary of the temple and bewailed to the image of the god the danger which was impending over him; and as he was thus lamenting, sleep came upon him, and it seemed to him in his vision that the god came and stood by him and encouraged him, saying that he should suffer no evil if he went forth to meet the army of the Arabians; for he himself would send him helpers. Trusting in these things seen in sleep, he took with him, they said, those of the Egyptians who were willing to follow him, and encamped in Pelusion, for by this way the invasion came: and not one of the warrior class followed him, but shop-keepers and artisans and men of the market.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.141.

passages.text: Then after they came, there swarmed by night upon their enemies mice of the fields, and ate up their quivers and their bows, and moreover the handles of their shields, so that on the next day they fled, and being without defence of arms great numbers fell. And at the present time this king stands in the temple of Hephaistos in stone, holding upon his hand a mouse, and by letters inscribed he says these words: 'Let him who looks upon me learn to fear the gods.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.141.

title.en: The Sun Rose Where It Sets: Egypt's Twice-Changed Sky
title.zh: 日出改處：埃及天空四度之變

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (the priests' reckoning of eleven thousand years)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（祭司所記一萬一千年之推算）

texts.period: Priests' cosmological account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.142 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 142

summary.en: The priests of Thebes, counting 341 generations of kings and chief-priests, declare that within those eleven thousand years no god ever appeared in human form — but the sun moved four times from his accustomed place of rising: twice rising where he now sets, and twice setting where he now rises; meanwhile nothing in Egypt changed — not the fruits of the earth, nor the river, nor diseases, nor deaths.
summary.zh: 底比斯祭司推算三百四十一代王與大祭司，共一萬一千年，其間從無神以人形顯現——惟太陽四度改其常規出沒之地：今沒處曾兩度為其出處，今出處曾兩度為其沒處；而其間埃及百物不變——土地所產、河之水、疾病、死亡，皆如故。

sensitivity.note: Ancient cosmological report via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Read by some as a memory of precessional or calendrical shifts.

passages.text: So far in the story the Egyptians and the priests were they who made the report, declaring that from the first king down to this priest of Hephaistos who reigned last, there had been three hundred and forty-one generations of men, and that in them there had been the same number of chief-priests and of kings: but three hundred generations of men are equal to ten thousand years, for a hundred years is three generations of men; and in the one-and-forty generations which remain, those I mean which were added to the three hundred, there are one thousand three hundred and forty years. Thus in the period of eleven thousand three hundred and forty years they said that there had arisen no god in human form.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.142.

passages.text: In this time they said that the sun had moved four times from his accustomed place of rising, and where he now sets he had thence twice had his rising, and in the place from whence he now rises he had twice had his setting; and in the meantime nothing in Egypt had been changed from its usual state, neither that which comes from the earth nor that which comes to them from the river nor that which concerns diseases or deaths.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.142.

title.en: The Floating Island of Chemmis: Where Leto Gave Birth
title.zh: 克米斯浮島：勒托誕子之處

region.en: Chemmis, near Buto, Nile Delta, Egypt (the floating island in the deep water)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布托附近克米斯（深水中的浮島）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.156 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 156

summary.en: In the deep water near Buto floats the island of Chemmis, drifting wherever the river carries it; there, the Egyptians say, Leto received and secretly nursed Apollo and Artemis when in fear of Typhon — at her request Poseidon anchored it with four diamond-footed anchors hidden under the water, and the island still moves, and no one may set foot on it.
summary.zh: 布托附近深水中有浮島克米斯，隨河漂移；埃及人言：勒托懼提豐，攜阿波羅與阿爾忒彌斯至此隱匿哺育——應其請，波塞冬以四枚鑽石足之錨沉於水下繫島，故島雖浮而不得行，且無人得踏上其土。

sensitivity.note: Ancient place-myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The Egyptian name Chemmis (Akh-biten) matches the 'hidden nest of Horus' of the Isis cycle.

passages.text: This house then of all the things that were to be seen by me in that temple is the most marvellous, and among those which come next is the island called Chemmis. This is situated in a deep and broad lake near by in Thebes, and the Egyptians say that it is a floating island. I will set down how it is according to the account given to me, and in what manner it moves: the Egyptians say that in this island, which was not previously fixed or made fast to the mainland, Leto, one of the eight gods first existing, dwelling in Buto where this oracle of hers is, received Apollo and Artemis from Isis, and hid them for safety from Typhon, and supported and concealed them there.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.156 (the house-of-single-stone introduction trimmed).

title.en: The Courtesan Rhodopis and Her Pyramid: A Slander Corrected
title.zh: 名妓羅多庇斯與其金字塔：闢謠

region.en: Naucratis, Egypt (the courtesans' city; Delphi for the iron spits)
region.zh: 埃及諾克拉提斯（名妓之城；鐵籤則獻於德爾菲）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.134-135 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 134-135

summary.en: Greeks said the third pyramid was built by the courtesan Rhodopis; Herodotus, who knew better, corrects the tale: Rhodopis of Thrace — fellow-slave of Aesop the fable-maker, ransomed by Charaxos, brother of Sappho — was famous in Amasis' reign, centuries too late; her tithe went not to a pyramid but to iron spits of ox-piercing size, dedicated at Delphi, where they still lay in his day.
summary.zh: 希臘人謂第三金字塔為名妓羅多庇斯所建；希羅多德闢之：色雷斯女奴羅多庇斯——寓言家伊索的同門奴、薩福之弟卡拉克索斯贖其身——盛名在阿馬西斯之世，晚於建塔之王數百年；其什一之財非建塔，乃鑄巨鐵籤獻於德爾菲，希氏時猶陳於廟後。

sensitivity.note: Ancient biographical legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: This pyramid some of the Hellenes say was built by the courtesan Rhodopis, not therein speaking rightly: and besides this it is evident to me that they who speak thus do not even know who Rhodopis was, for otherwise they would not have attributed to her the building of a pyramid like this, on which have been spent (so to speak) innumerable thousands of talents: moreover they do not know that Rhodopis flourished in the reign of Amasis, and not in this king's reign; for Rhodopis lived very many years later than the kings who left behind the pyramids. By descent she was of Thrace, and she was a slave of Iadmon the son of Hephaistopolis a Samian, and a fellow-slave of Esop the maker of fables.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.134.

passages.text: As for Rhodopis, she came to Egypt brought by Xanthes the Samian, and having come thither to exercise her calling she was redeemed from slavery for a great sum by a man of Mytilene, Charaxos son of Scamandronymos and brother of Sappho the lyric poet. Thus was Rhodopis set free, and she remained in Egypt and by her beauty won so much liking that she made great gain of money for one like Rhodopis, though not enough to suffice for the cost of such a pyramid as this.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.135.

passages.text: Rhodopis wished to leave behind her a memorial of herself in Hellas, namely to cause a thing to be made such as happens not to have been thought of or dedicated in a temple by any besides, and to dedicate this at Delphi as a memorial of herself. Accordingly with the tithe of her wealth she caused to be made spits of iron of size large enough to pierce a whole ox, and many in number, going as far therein as her tithe allowed her, and she sent them to Delphi: these are even at the present time lying there, heaped all together behind the altar which the Chians dedicated.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.135.
